topics.title: Set operations and relations
topics.summary: Union, intersection, complement, De Morgan's laws, and properties of relations.
notes: De Morgan's laws: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′.
|A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| for finite sets.
A relation R on a set A is reflexive if aRa for every a; symmetric if aRb implies bRa; transitive if aRb and bRc imply aRc. A relation with all three properties is an equivalence relation.
outcomes: Decide whether a relation is an equivalence relation

lesson.hook: In a class of 60, 35 like cricket and 30 like football. Can you be sure some like both?
lesson.example:
Class of 60: |C| = 35, |F| = 30, |C ∩ F| = 10.
|C ∪ F| = 35 + 30 − 10 = 55, so 60 − 55 = 5 students like neither.

questions.q: If |A| = 20, |B| = 15 and |A ∪ B| = 28, find |A ∩ B|.
Is "is a sibling of" (excluding oneself) an equivalence relation?

topics.title: Functions
topics.summary: One-one, onto and bijective functions, composition and inverse.
notes: A function f: A → B assigns exactly one element of B to each element of A.
f is one-one (injective) if f(a) = f(b) implies a = b; onto (surjective) if every element of B has a pre-image; bijective if both.
Only a bijection has an inverse f⁻¹: B → A.
Composition: (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)); in general g ∘ f ≠ f ∘ g.
outcomes: Classify a function as injective, surjective or bijective

topics.title: Propositions and truth tables
topics.summary: Connectives, truth tables, tautologies and logical equivalence.
notes: The conditional p → q is false only when p is true and q is false; p → q is equivalent to ¬p ∨ q.
The biconditional p ↔ q is true when p and q have the same truth value.
A tautology is true for every assignment of truth values; a contradiction is false for every assignment.
outcomes: Test whether two statements are logically equivalent

topics.title: Quantifiers and counting
topics.summary: Predicates, universal and existential quantifiers, and the basic counting principles.
notes: ∀x P(x) is true when P(x) holds for every x; ∃x P(x) when it holds for at least one x.
Negation: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x).
Permutations: nPr = n! ÷ (n − r)!; combinations: nCr = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!).
Pigeonhole principle: if n + 1 objects go into n boxes, some box holds at least two.

topics.title: Matrix operations and determinants
topics.summary: Types of matrices, addition, multiplication, transpose, determinant and inverse.
notes: Matrices A (m × n) and B (n × p) can be multiplied; AB is m × p, and in general AB ≠ BA.
For a 2 × 2 matrix [a b; c d], the determinant is ad − bc.
A square matrix has an inverse if and only if its determinant is non-zero: A⁻¹ = adj(A) ÷ |A|.
(AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ; a matrix is symmetric if Aᵀ = A.
outcomes: Find the inverse of a 2 × 2 or 3 × 3 matrix

topics.title: Graphs and degrees
topics.summary: Vertices, edges, degree, and the handshaking lemma.
notes: Handshaking lemma: the sum of the degrees of all vertices of a graph is twice the number of edges.
Consequently, every graph has an even number of vertices of odd degree.
A graph is simple if it has no loops or parallel edges; the complete graph Kₙ has n(n − 1)/2 edges.
outcomes: Count the edges of complete and regular graphs

topics.title: Euler and Hamilton graphs, and trees
topics.summary: Euler circuits, Hamiltonian cycles, and the properties of trees.
notes: A connected graph has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree; it has an Euler path (not circuit) if exactly two vertices have odd degree.
A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex exactly once; no simple degree test decides it in general.
A tree is a connected graph with no cycles; a tree with n vertices has n − 1 edges.
A spanning tree of a connected graph includes all its vertices with the fewest edges.
outcomes: Decide whether a graph has an Euler path or circuit

courses.title: Problem Solving Techniques (C Programming), BCA Semester 1

topics.title: Algorithms, flowcharts and pseudocode
topics.summary: What an algorithm is, its properties, and how to express it.
notes: An algorithm is a finite sequence of unambiguous steps that solves a problem; it has input, output, definiteness, finiteness and effectiveness.
A flowchart uses standard symbols: oval (start/stop), parallelogram (input/output), rectangle (process), diamond (decision).
Pseudocode states the steps in structured English, independent of any language.
Fundamental algorithms: exchanging two values, counting, summation, factorial, Fibonacci series, reversing digits.
outcomes: Write an algorithm and a flowchart for a simple problem

lesson.hook: How would you tell a robot to find the largest of three numbers?
lesson.example:
Algorithm to swap a and b: 1. temp ← a  2. a ← b  3. b ← temp.
Trace a = 4, b = 9: temp = 4, a = 9, b = 4.

questions.q: List the five properties of an algorithm.
Which flowchart symbol is used for a decision?

topics.title: Factoring and array techniques
topics.summary: Classic problem-solving algorithms on numbers and arrays.
notes: The smallest divisor of n need only be searched up to √n; if none divides n, n is prime.
GCD by Euclid's algorithm: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), and gcd(a, 0) = a.
Array techniques: finding the maximum, reversing in place (swap a[i] with a[n−1−i]), removing duplicates, counting frequencies.

topics.title: Structure of a C program, tokens and data types
topics.summary: The parts of a C program, its tokens, and basic data types.
notes: A C program has preprocessor directives, global declarations, the main() function and other functions; execution starts at main().
Tokens: keywords, identifiers, constants, strings, operators and special symbols.
Basic types: int, char, float, double; qualifiers short, long, signed, unsigned. sizeof gives a type's size in bytes.
Symbolic constants are defined with #define or const.
outcomes: Identify the parts and tokens of a C program
Declare and initialise variables of suitable types

topics.title: Operators, expressions and I/O
topics.summary: Operators, precedence, type conversion and formatted input/output.
notes: Operator classes: arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment, increment/decrement, conditional (?:), bitwise and special.
Integer division truncates: 7 / 2 is 3, and 7 % 2 is 1.
printf and scanf use format specifiers: %d int, %f float, %lf double, %c char, %s string; scanf needs the address (&x) of non-array variables.
Unformatted I/O: getchar, putchar, gets (unsafe, prefer fgets), puts.
outcomes: Read and print data with printf and scanf

questions.q: What is the value of 5 + 3 * 2 % 4 in C?

topics.title: Decision making and loops
topics.summary: if, if-else, switch, while, do-while, for, break and continue.
notes: switch selects among integer or character cases; without break, control falls through to the next case.
while tests before the body; do-while runs the body at least once; for combines initialisation, test and update.
break leaves the innermost loop or switch; continue skips to the next iteration.
outcomes: Choose the right control structure for a problem
Write nested loops to print patterns

lesson.hook: An ATM keeps asking for your PIN until it is right or you have tried three times. Which loop is that?
lesson.example:
Sum of digits of 472: while (n > 0) { s += n % 10; n /= 10; }
Trace: s = 2, n = 47; s = 9, n = 4; s = 13, n = 0. Sum is 13.

questions.q: How many times does for (i = 0; i < 10; i += 3) run?
Which loop always executes at least once?

lesson.homework: Write a program that prints all prime numbers between 1 and 100.

topics.title: Arrays and strings
topics.summary: One- and two-dimensional arrays, and strings as character arrays.
notes: Array indices run from 0 to n − 1; C does not check bounds.
A 2-D array int a[3][4] is stored row by row (row-major order).
A string is a char array ending in '\0'; string.h gives strlen, strcpy, strcat, strcmp.
outcomes: Process arrays with loops (search, sum, matrix operations)

topics.title: Functions and recursion
topics.summary: Defining functions, parameter passing, scope and recursion.
notes: A function has a prototype (declaration), a definition and calls; return gives one value back.
C passes arguments by value; to change a caller's variable, pass its address (call by reference through pointers).
Storage classes: auto, register, static (keeps its value between calls) and extern.
A recursive function calls itself and needs a base case: fact(n) = n × fact(n − 1), fact(0) = 1.
outcomes: Write and call functions with parameters
Write recursive functions with a correct base case

topics.title: Pointers
topics.summary: Addresses, pointer arithmetic, and pointers with arrays and functions.
notes: & gives the address of a variable; * dereferences a pointer.
For int *p, p + 1 points to the next int (address increases by sizeof(int)).
An array name is a pointer to its first element: a[i] is *(a + i).
malloc, calloc, realloc and free (stdlib.h) manage dynamic memory.
outcomes: Use pointers to pass arguments by reference

topics.title: Structures, unions and command-line arguments
topics.summary: Grouping data with struct and union, and reading arguments from main.
notes: A struct groups members of different types; members are accessed with . (or -> through a pointer).
A union's members share one memory location; its size is that of its largest member.
main(int argc, char *argv[]) receives command-line arguments; argv[0] is the program name.
outcomes: Define structures and arrays of structures

topics.title: Number systems and conversions
topics.summary: Binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal numbers and converting between them.
notes: Bases: binary 2, octal 8, decimal 10, hexadecimal 16 (digits 0–9, A–F).
Decimal to binary: divide repeatedly by 2 and read the remainders from bottom to top.
One octal digit is three bits; one hexadecimal digit is four bits.
Two's complement of a binary number = one's complement + 1; it represents negative numbers.

lesson.hook: Why does a computer show 255 as FF?

questions.q: Convert 1011 1110 to hexadecimal.
Find the 8-bit two's complement of 0000 0101.

topics.title: Codes
topics.summary: BCD, excess-3, Gray code, ASCII and Unicode.
notes: BCD codes each decimal digit in 4 bits: 59 is 0101 1001.
Excess-3 code = BCD + 3 (0011); it is self-complementing.
In Gray code successive values differ in one bit; binary to Gray: g = b XOR (b shifted right by one).
ASCII is a 7-bit code (128 characters); Unicode covers all scripts.
outcomes: Represent numbers in BCD, excess-3 and Gray code
Convert between binary and Gray code

topics.title: Logic gates
topics.summary: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR, with their truth tables.
notes: AND outputs 1 only if all inputs are 1; OR outputs 1 if any input is 1; NOT inverts.
NAND and NOR are universal gates: any circuit can be built from either alone.
XOR outputs 1 when the inputs differ; XNOR when they are equal.
outcomes: Write truth tables of the basic and universal gates
Build NOT, AND and OR from NAND gates

topics.title: Boolean algebra and K-maps
topics.summary: Boolean laws, De Morgan's theorems, SOP/POS forms and Karnaugh-map simplification.
notes: De Morgan: (A·B)′ = A′ + B′ and (A + B)′ = A′·B′.
Absorption: A + AB = A; A(A + B) = A.
Sum of products (minterms) and product of sums (maxterms) are canonical forms.
In a K-map, group adjacent 1s in powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8) as large as possible; each group gives one product term.
outcomes: Minimise functions of up to four variables with K-maps

questions.q: Simplify A·B + A·B′.

topics.title: Combinational circuits
topics.summary: Adders, subtractors, multiplexers, demultiplexers, encoders and decoders.
notes: Half adder: Sum = A XOR B, Carry = A·B. Full adder adds three bits: Sum = A XOR B XOR Cin.
A multiplexer selects one of 2ⁿ inputs using n select lines; a demultiplexer does the reverse.
A decoder converts n inputs to up to 2ⁿ outputs; an encoder does the reverse.
outcomes: Design a half adder and a full adder

topics.title: Flip-flops, registers and counters
topics.summary: SR, JK, D and T flip-flops, and their use in registers and counters.
notes: A flip-flop stores one bit; it changes state on a clock edge.
SR: S = R = 1 is not allowed. JK: J = K = 1 toggles. D: output follows D. T: toggles when T = 1.
Shift registers move bits on each clock (SISO, SIPO, PISO, PIPO).
An n-bit ripple counter counts 0 to 2ⁿ − 1; each flip-flop is clocked by the previous one.

topics.title: CPU, instructions and addressing modes
topics.summary: Basic computer organisation, registers, instruction cycle and addressing modes.
notes: Main units: input, output, memory, ALU and control unit; ALU and control unit form the CPU.
Key registers: PC (address of next instruction), IR (current instruction), MAR, MDR, accumulator.
Instruction cycle: fetch, decode, execute (and store).
Addressing modes: immediate, direct, indirect, register, register indirect, indexed, relative.

topics.title: Memory organisation
topics.summary: Memory hierarchy, RAM and ROM, cache and virtual memory.
notes: Hierarchy (fastest to slowest): registers, cache, main memory, secondary storage.
RAM is volatile (SRAM for cache, DRAM for main memory); ROM, PROM, EPROM and EEPROM are non-volatile.
Cache works by locality of reference; hit ratio = hits ÷ (hits + misses).
Cache mapping: direct, associative and set-associative.

topics.title: Data structures and algorithm analysis
topics.summary: Classification of data structures, abstract data types and Big-O notation.
notes: Linear structures: arrays, stacks, queues, linked lists; non-linear: trees and graphs.
An abstract data type specifies data and operations, not implementation.
Big-O gives an upper bound on growth: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ).
Time–space trade-off: faster algorithms often need more memory.
outcomes: Find the time complexity of simple loops

lesson.hook: Finding a name in a phone book of a million names: page by page, or by opening in the middle?
lesson.example:
for (i = 0; i < n; i++) for (j = 0; j < n; j++) count++; runs n × n times: O(n²).
while (n > 1) n = n / 2; runs about log₂ n times: O(log n).

questions.q: What is the complexity of a single loop over n elements?

topics.title: Searching
topics.summary: Linear and binary search.
notes: Linear search checks each element: O(n); works on unsorted data.
Binary search needs sorted data; it compares with the middle element and halves the range: O(log n).
mid = low + (high − low) / 2 avoids overflow.

questions.q: How many comparisons at most does binary search need for 1,024 elements?

topics.title: Sorting
topics.summary: Bubble, selection, insertion, merge and quick sort.
notes: Bubble, selection and insertion sort are O(n²); insertion sort is O(n) on nearly sorted data.
Merge sort divides, sorts and merges: O(n log n) always, but needs O(n) extra space.
Quick sort partitions around a pivot: O(n log n) on average, O(n²) in the worst case.
A sort is stable if equal keys keep their relative order (merge and insertion are stable; quick and selection are not).
outcomes: Trace each sorting algorithm on an example
Choose a sort for a given situation

lesson.example:
Bubble sort 5 1 4 2, pass 1: 1 5 4 2 → 1 4 5 2 → 1 4 2 5 (largest at the end).
Pass 2: 1 4 2 5 → 1 2 4 5. Pass 3 makes no swaps, so it stops.

topics.title: Stacks
topics.summary: LIFO stacks, push and pop, and expression conversion and evaluation.
notes: A stack is last in, first out: push adds to the top, pop removes from the top.
Overflow: push on a full stack; underflow: pop on an empty stack.
Uses: function calls and recursion, undo, infix to postfix conversion, postfix evaluation, bracket matching.
Postfix evaluation: push operands; on an operator pop two, apply, push the result.
outcomes: Implement a stack with an array and a linked list
Convert infix to postfix and evaluate postfix

questions.q: Evaluate the postfix 2 3 4 * +.

topics.title: Queues
topics.summary: Linear, circular and priority queues, and deques.
notes: A queue is first in, first out: insert at the rear, delete at the front.
A circular queue reuses freed space: rear = (rear + 1) % size.
A priority queue serves the highest priority first; a deque allows insertion and deletion at both ends.

topics.title: Singly, doubly and circular linked lists
topics.summary: Nodes and pointers; insertion, deletion and traversal.
notes: A node holds data and a pointer to the next node; the list is reached through a head pointer.
Insertion and deletion are O(1) once the position is known; access by index is O(n).
A doubly linked list has next and previous pointers; a circular list's last node points back to the first.
Linked lists grow dynamically, unlike fixed-size arrays.
outcomes: Insert and delete nodes at any position

topics.title: Binary trees and binary search trees
topics.summary: Tree terminology, traversals and BST operations.
notes: A binary tree node has at most two children; a tree of height h has at most 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes (root at height 0).
Traversals: inorder (L, root, R), preorder (root, L, R), postorder (L, R, root).
In a BST, left subtree keys < node < right subtree keys; inorder traversal gives sorted order.
BST search, insert and delete are O(h): O(log n) when balanced, O(n) when skewed.
outcomes: Traverse a binary tree in all three orders
Insert into and delete from a BST

topics.title: Graph representation and traversal
topics.summary: Adjacency matrix and list, BFS and DFS.
notes: Adjacency matrix uses O(V²) space; adjacency list uses O(V + E).
BFS visits level by level using a queue; DFS goes deep first using a stack or recursion.
BFS finds shortest paths (by number of edges) in unweighted graphs.

courses.title: Object Oriented Programming using Java, BCA Semester 2

topics.title: OOP principles
topics.summary: Objects, classes, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction.
notes: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance with state (fields) and behaviour (methods).
Encapsulation hides data behind methods; abstraction shows only essential features.
Inheritance lets a class reuse another's members; polymorphism lets one interface have many forms.
outcomes: Explain the four pillars of OOP with examples

topics.title: Java platform and language basics
topics.summary: JDK, JRE, JVM, bytecode, data types and control statements.
notes: javac compiles source to platform-independent bytecode (.class); the JVM interprets or JIT-compiles it ("write once, run anywhere").
JDK = JRE + development tools; JRE = JVM + class libraries.
Primitive types: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char (16-bit Unicode), boolean.
Arrays are objects with a length field; Java checks array bounds at run time.
outcomes: Compile and run a Java program
Use Java's data types, operators and control statements

topics.title: Classes, constructors and methods
topics.summary: Defining classes, constructors, overloading, this and static.
notes: A constructor has the class's name and no return type; if none is written Java supplies a default one.
Method overloading: same name, different parameter lists (compile-time polymorphism).
this refers to the current object; static members belong to the class, not to objects.
Access modifiers: private, default (package), protected, public.
outcomes: Write classes with constructors and overloaded methods

lesson.hook: Every student has a name and marks, but each student's values differ. How does one class describe them all?
lesson.example:
class Student { String name; int marks; Student(String n, int m) { name = n; marks = m; } boolean passed() { return marks >= 40; } }
Student s = new Student("Asha", 72); s.passed() returns true.

questions.q: What is printed by: int[] a = {1, 2, 3}; System.out.println(a.length);
Can a constructor return a value?
questions.a: No; it has no return type.

topics.title: Inheritance and polymorphism
topics.summary: extends, super, method overriding, abstract classes and final.
notes: Java supports single, multilevel and hierarchical inheritance of classes; multiple inheritance only through interfaces.
super calls the parent's constructor or methods.
Overriding: a subclass method with the same signature; the call is resolved at run time (dynamic method dispatch).
An abstract class cannot be instantiated; final prevents overriding (methods) or inheritance (classes).

topics.title: Interfaces and packages
topics.summary: Defining and implementing interfaces; creating and importing packages.
notes: An interface declares methods a class must implement; a class can implement many interfaces.
Interface fields are public static final; methods are abstract unless default or static.
Packages group classes and control access; import brings them into scope.

topics.title: Exception handling
topics.summary: try, catch, finally, throw and throws; checked and unchecked exceptions.
notes: Checked exceptions (e.g. IOException) must be caught or declared with throws; unchecked ones extend RuntimeException.
finally runs whether or not an exception occurs.
Custom exceptions extend Exception.

topics.title: Multithreading
topics.summary: Creating threads, thread life cycle and synchronisation.
notes: Create a thread by extending Thread or implementing Runnable; start() runs run() on a new thread.
Life cycle: new, runnable, running, blocked/waiting, terminated.
synchronized methods or blocks let only one thread at a time hold an object's lock.

topics.title: Event handling and GUI basics
topics.summary: AWT/Swing components and the delegation event model.
notes: In the delegation event model a source generates events and registered listeners handle them.
Swing components (JFrame, JButton, JTextField) are lightweight; layout managers (FlowLayout, BorderLayout, GridLayout) arrange them.
ActionListener's actionPerformed handles button clicks.

topics.title: Database systems and architecture
topics.summary: Files versus DBMS, the three-schema architecture, data independence and DBMS users.
notes: A DBMS reduces redundancy and inconsistency, enforces integrity and security, and supports concurrent access.
Three-schema architecture: internal (physical), conceptual (logical) and external (view) levels.
Logical data independence: change the conceptual schema without changing views; physical: change storage without changing the conceptual schema.
Data models: hierarchical, network, relational, object-oriented.
outcomes: Explain the advantages of a DBMS over files

lesson.hook: A college keeps student details in three separate Excel files. A student changes phone number. What can go wrong?

questions.q: What is physical data independence?
questions.a: Changing how data is stored without changing the conceptual schema or programs.

topics.title: ER diagrams
topics.summary: Entities, attributes, relationships, cardinality and participation.
notes: Entity sets are rectangles, attributes ovals, relationship sets diamonds; key attributes are underlined.
Attribute kinds: simple/composite, single/multivalued (double oval), derived (dashed oval).
Cardinality ratios: 1:1, 1:N, M:N; total participation is a double line.
A weak entity (double rectangle) has no key of its own and depends on an owner entity.
outcomes: Draw an ER diagram from a description
Convert an ER diagram to tables

topics.title: Keys and integrity constraints
topics.summary: Relations, tuples, attributes, and the kinds of keys.
notes: A relation is a table; a tuple is a row; an attribute is a column; the domain is the set of allowed values.
Super key: any set of attributes that identifies a tuple; candidate key: a minimal super key; primary key: the chosen candidate key.
A foreign key refers to the primary key of another relation (referential integrity).
Entity integrity: a primary key cannot be NULL.
outcomes: Identify candidate, primary and foreign keys

topics.title: Relational algebra
topics.summary: Select, project, union, difference, Cartesian product and join.
notes: σ (select) picks rows; π (project) picks columns.
Union, intersection and difference need union-compatible relations.
A natural join combines rows with equal values in common attributes.
outcomes: Translate simple English queries into algebra and SQL

questions.q: Write the algebra for the names of students with marks over 80.

topics.title: Functional dependencies and normal forms
topics.summary: Anomalies, functional dependencies, and 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF.
notes: Redundancy causes insertion, deletion and update anomalies.
X → Y means each X value determines exactly one Y value.
1NF: atomic values. 2NF: 1NF and no partial dependency on a composite key. 3NF: 2NF and no transitive dependency of non-key attributes. BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key.
Decomposition should be lossless and preserve dependencies.
outcomes: Find functional dependencies in a table

lesson.hook: Why does one student's address appear 6 times in the marks table?
lesson.example:
Marks(RollNo, Subject, Name, Grade): key (RollNo, Subject); RollNo → Name is a partial dependency.
2NF: Student(RollNo, Name) and Marks(RollNo, Subject, Grade).

questions.q: Which normal form removes transitive dependencies?

topics.title: DDL, DML and constraints
topics.summary: Creating tables and changing data with SQL.
notes: DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE; DML: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE; DCL: GRANT, REVOKE; TCL: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT.
Constraints: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT.
DELETE removes chosen rows and can be rolled back; TRUNCATE removes all rows quickly; DROP removes the table.

topics.title: Queries, joins and aggregates
topics.summary: SELECT with WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, joins and subqueries.
notes: Clause order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY.
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.
Joins: INNER, LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER; a subquery is a query inside another.
outcomes: Write queries with joins and aggregates

lesson.example: SELECT dept, AVG(salary) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000 ORDER BY dept;

questions.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
questions.a: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

topics.title: Transactions and concurrency control
topics.summary: ACID properties, schedules, serialisability, locking and recovery.
notes: ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability.
A schedule is serialisable if it is equivalent to some serial schedule.
Two-phase locking (growing then shrinking phase) guarantees conflict serialisability.
Problems without control: lost update, dirty read, unrepeatable read. Recovery uses logs (undo/redo) and checkpoints.

topics.title: .NET architecture
topics.summary: CLR, CTS, CLS, MSIL, JIT compilation and assemblies.
notes: Source code compiles to MSIL (CIL); the CLR's JIT compiler turns it into native code at run time.
The CTS defines the types all .NET languages share; the CLS is the subset every language must support.
The CLR provides memory management (garbage collection), type safety and exception handling.
An assembly (.exe or .dll) contains IL code, metadata and a manifest.
outcomes: Explain the roles of the CLR, CTS and CLS

topics.title: C# language basics
topics.summary: Types, boxing, control statements, arrays and strings.
notes: Value types (int, double, struct, enum) live on the stack; reference types (class, string, array) on the heap.
Boxing converts a value type to object; unboxing converts it back with a cast.
foreach iterates over arrays and collections; strings are immutable.
outcomes: Write C# programs with control structures and arrays

topics.title: Classes, inheritance and interfaces in C#
topics.summary: Properties, constructors, inheritance, virtual/override, interfaces, delegates and events.
notes: Properties wrap fields with get and set accessors.
A method must be virtual in the base class to be overridden with override.
A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method; events are built on delegates.

topics.title: Windows Forms and ADO.NET
topics.summary: Building forms with controls, and connecting to a database with ADO.NET.
notes: Windows Forms apps use controls (Button, TextBox, Label, DataGridView) with event handlers.
ADO.NET objects: Connection, Command, DataReader (connected, forward-only) and DataAdapter with DataSet (disconnected).
ASP.NET builds web pages with server controls and code-behind files.
outcomes: Build a simple Windows Forms application
Read and update a database with ADO.NET

topics.title: Network models
topics.summary: Network types, topologies and the OSI and TCP/IP models.
notes: Network types: PAN, LAN, MAN, WAN; topologies: bus, star, ring, mesh, tree.
OSI layers (bottom up): physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application.
TCP/IP layers: network access, internet, transport, application.
Each layer adds a header (encapsulation); units: bits, frames, packets, segments.
outcomes: Name the OSI layers and their functions
Compare the OSI and TCP/IP models

topics.title: Transmission media and signals
topics.summary: Guided and unguided media, bandwidth, and multiplexing.
notes: Guided media: twisted pair, coaxial cable, optical fibre; unguided: radio, microwave, infrared.
Optical fibre uses total internal reflection; it has high bandwidth and is immune to electromagnetic interference.
Multiplexing shares a link: FDM (frequency), TDM (time), WDM (wavelength, for fibre).
Switching: circuit, message and packet switching.

topics.title: Error detection and flow control
topics.summary: Framing, parity, CRC, and stop-and-wait and sliding-window protocols.
notes: Single parity detects odd numbers of bit errors; CRC divides by a generator polynomial and appends the remainder.
Hamming code can correct single-bit errors.
Stop-and-wait sends one frame per acknowledgement; sliding window (Go-Back-N, Selective Repeat) sends several.
MAC protocols: ALOHA, CSMA/CD (Ethernet), CSMA/CA (Wi-Fi).

topics.title: IP addressing and routing
topics.summary: IPv4 addresses, classes, subnetting and routing algorithms.
notes: An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four decimal octets; IPv6 is 128 bits.
Classful ranges: A 1–126, B 128–191, C 192–223 (first octet); CIDR notation /n gives the network prefix length.
A /24 network has 2⁸ − 2 = 254 usable host addresses.
Routing: distance vector (Bellman-Ford, RIP) and link state (Dijkstra, OSPF).
outcomes: Find network and broadcast addresses from an IP and mask

questions.q: How many usable hosts does a /26 subnet have?

topics.title: TCP, UDP and application protocols
topics.summary: Ports, TCP and UDP, and DNS, HTTP, SMTP and FTP.
notes: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable (three-way handshake, acknowledgements); UDP is connectionless and faster.
Well-known ports: HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, FTP 21, SMTP 25, DNS 53, SSH 22.
DNS maps domain names to IP addresses.

topics.title: Data types, operators and control flow
topics.summary: Variables, built-in types, operators, if-elif-else, while and for.
notes: Python is interpreted and dynamically typed; indentation marks blocks.
Built-in types: int, float, complex, bool, str, list, tuple, set, dict, None.
// is floor division, ** is power, % is remainder; 7 // 2 is 3 and 2 ** 3 is 8.
range(start, stop, step) stops before stop; for loops may have an else that runs if no break occurs.
outcomes: Write programs with conditions and loops

lesson.hook: The same 'find the average' program in C needs 15 lines. How short can it be in Python?
lesson.example:
marks = [72, 85, 64]; print(sum(marks) / len(marks)) prints 73.666…
for i in range(1, 10, 3): print(i) prints 1, 4, 7.

questions.q: What does 17 // 5 give? And 17 % 5?
What does list(range(5, 0, -2)) give?

topics.title: Functions, arguments and scope
topics.summary: def, return, default and keyword arguments, *args, **kwargs, lambda and recursion.
notes: Default arguments are evaluated once, when the function is defined (so avoid mutable defaults).
*args collects extra positional arguments as a tuple; **kwargs collects keyword arguments as a dict.
lambda creates a small anonymous function: lambda x: x * x.
LEGB rule for names: local, enclosing, global, built-in.
outcomes: Define functions with different argument kinds

topics.title: Modules and packages
topics.summary: import, standard modules and creating your own modules.
notes: A module is a .py file; a package is a folder of modules (with __init__.py).
import math; from math import sqrt; import numpy as np.
if __name__ == '__main__': runs code only when the file is executed directly.

topics.title: Strings, lists and tuples
topics.summary: Indexing, slicing, methods, list comprehensions and immutability.
notes: Indexing starts at 0; negative indices count from the end; s[a:b] runs from a up to b − 1.
Lists are mutable; tuples and strings are immutable.
List comprehension: [x * x for x in range(5) if x % 2 == 0] gives [0, 4, 16].
Common list methods: append, extend, insert, remove, pop, sort, reverse.

questions.q: For s = 'PYTHON', what is s[1:4]?

topics.title: Sets and dictionaries
topics.summary: Set operations, dictionary methods and iteration.
notes: A set holds unique, unordered items: | union, & intersection, − difference.
A dict maps unique, immutable keys to values; d.get(k, default) avoids KeyError.
Iterate with for k, v in d.items().
outcomes: Use sets and dictionaries to solve problems
Count word frequencies with a dictionary

topics.title: File handling and exception handling
topics.summary: Opening, reading and writing files, and try-except-else-finally.
notes: Modes: 'r' read, 'w' write (truncates), 'a' append, 'b' binary.
with open(name) as f: closes the file automatically.
try-except catches errors; else runs if no exception; finally always runs; raise throws an exception.
outcomes: Read and write text and CSV files

topics.title: Classes and objects in Python
topics.summary: class, __init__, self, inheritance and special methods.
notes: __init__ initialises a new object; self is the instance.
Inheritance: class Child(Parent); super().__init__() calls the parent's constructor.
Special methods such as __str__ and __len__ customise built-in behaviour.

topics.title: NumPy, pandas and Matplotlib
topics.summary: Arrays, data frames and plotting for data analysis.
notes: NumPy arrays are homogeneous and support vectorised operations: np.array([1, 2]) * 2 gives [2, 4].
pandas: Series (1-D) and DataFrame (2-D); read_csv, head, describe, groupby.
Matplotlib's pyplot draws line, bar, scatter and pie charts.
outcomes: Load and summarise a dataset with pandas

topics.title: Operating system concepts
topics.summary: Functions and types of operating systems, system calls and OS structure.
notes: An OS manages processes, memory, files, devices and security, and provides the user interface.
Types: batch, multiprogramming, time-sharing, real-time, distributed, mobile.
System calls are the interface between programs and the kernel (e.g. fork, exec, read, write).
Kernel designs: monolithic, layered, microkernel.
outcomes: Describe the functions and types of operating systems
Explain how a system call works

topics.title: Processes and threads
topics.summary: Process states, the PCB, context switching and threads.
notes: Process states: new, ready, running, waiting, terminated.
The PCB stores a process's state, program counter, registers, scheduling and memory information.
A context switch saves one process's state and loads another's; it is pure overhead.
Threads of one process share code, data and files but have their own stack and registers.

topics.title: CPU scheduling
topics.summary: FCFS, SJF, priority and round robin scheduling; waiting and turnaround time.
notes: Turnaround time = Completion time − Arrival time; Waiting time = Turnaround time − Burst time.
FCFS can suffer the convoy effect; SJF gives the minimum average waiting time.
Round robin gives each process a time quantum in turn; good for time-sharing.
Priority scheduling can starve low-priority processes; aging fixes this.
outcomes: Draw Gantt charts and compute average waiting times

lesson.hook: Three people at a photocopier: one has 100 pages, two have 1 page each. Who should go first?
lesson.example:
FCFS, all arriving at 0: P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3. Waiting: 0, 24, 27; average 17.
SJF order P2, P3, P1: waiting 0, 3, 6; average 3.

questions.q: In round robin with quantum 4, how many turns does a 10 ms process need?

topics.title: Process synchronisation
topics.summary: Race conditions, critical sections, semaphores and classic problems.
notes: A critical-section solution needs mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.
A semaphore S is an integer with wait (P: S − 1, block if negative) and signal (V: S + 1).
Classic problems: producer–consumer, readers–writers, dining philosophers.

topics.title: Deadlocks
topics.summary: Deadlock conditions, prevention, avoidance (Banker's algorithm), detection and recovery.
notes: Four necessary conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait.
Prevention breaks one condition; avoidance (Banker's algorithm) grants a request only if the state stays safe.
Need = Max − Allocation; a safe sequence exists if every process can finish in some order.
outcomes: State and break the conditions for deadlock

topics.title: Memory management and virtual memory
topics.summary: Contiguous allocation, paging, segmentation and page replacement.
notes: Paging divides memory into fixed frames and processes into pages; it removes external fragmentation.
Logical address = (page number, offset); the page table maps pages to frames.
Page replacement: FIFO, optimal, LRU; FIFO can show Belady's anomaly.
Thrashing: the system spends more time paging than executing.
outcomes: Translate logical addresses with a page table
Count page faults for FIFO and LRU

topics.title: File systems and disk scheduling
topics.summary: File access and allocation methods, directories and disk scheduling.
notes: Access methods: sequential, direct, indexed.
Allocation: contiguous, linked, indexed.
Disk scheduling: FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN; seek time dominates disk access.
outcomes: Compute total head movement for disk scheduling algorithms

courses.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms, BCA Semester 5

topics.title: Asymptotic notation and recurrences
topics.summary: O, Ω and Θ notation, and solving recurrences.
notes: f(n) = O(g(n)) is an upper bound, Ω a lower bound and Θ a tight bound.
Master theorem for T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n): compare f(n) with n^(log_b a).
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n gives Θ(n log n); T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 gives Θ(log n).
outcomes: Express running times in asymptotic notation
Solve recurrences with the master theorem

topics.title: Divide and conquer
topics.summary: Binary search, merge sort, quick sort and Strassen's multiplication.
notes: Divide the problem, solve subproblems recursively, combine the results.
Merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n = Θ(n log n).
Strassen's method multiplies matrices in O(n^2.81) using 7 multiplications instead of 8.

topics.title: Greedy algorithms
topics.summary: Fractional knapsack, minimum spanning trees and Dijkstra's shortest paths.
notes: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step.
Fractional knapsack: take items in decreasing order of value per weight.
Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms find minimum spanning trees; Kruskal adds the cheapest edge that forms no cycle.
Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from one source when edge weights are non-negative.
outcomes: Find minimum spanning trees and shortest paths

topics.title: Dynamic programming
topics.summary: Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure; 0/1 knapsack, Floyd-Warshall, LCS.
notes: DP stores solutions of overlapping subproblems (memoisation or tabulation).
0/1 knapsack: K[i][w] = max(K[i−1][w], vᵢ + K[i−1][w − wᵢ]).
Floyd–Warshall finds all-pairs shortest paths in Θ(n³).

topics.title: Backtracking, branch and bound, and NP
topics.summary: N-queens, subset sum, and the classes P, NP and NP-complete.
notes: Backtracking builds solutions step by step and abandons a partial solution that cannot succeed.
Branch and bound prunes using bounds on the best possible solution.
P: solvable in polynomial time; NP: solutions verifiable in polynomial time; NP-complete problems (e.g. SAT, travelling salesman decision) are the hardest in NP.

courses.title: Statistical Computing and R Programming, BCA Semester 5

topics.title: R data types and structures
topics.summary: Vectors, matrices, lists, factors and data frames.
notes: The basic object is a vector; c(2, 4, 6) creates one; operations are vectorised.
Indexing starts at 1; x[-1] drops the first element.
matrix(), list(), factor() and data.frame() create the other structures; str() shows structure.
Assignment uses <- (or =).
outcomes: Create and manipulate R vectors and data frames
Import a CSV file into a data frame

topics.title: Measures of central tendency and dispersion
topics.summary: Mean, median, mode, range, variance and standard deviation.
notes: Mean x̄ = Σx ÷ n; median is the middle value of sorted data; mode is the most frequent value.
Sample variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1); standard deviation s = √s².
Coefficient of variation = (s ÷ x̄) × 100; lower CV means more consistent.
R: mean(x), median(x), var(x), sd(x), summary(x), quantile(x).
outcomes: Compute summary statistics by hand and in R
Compare the consistency of two data sets

lesson.hook: Two batsmen both average 50. One scores 48–52 every match; the other 0 or 100. Who would you pick?

questions.q: What does sd(c(1, 1, 1)) return in R?

topics.title: Binomial, Poisson and normal distributions
topics.summary: The common distributions and their R functions.
notes: Binomial: P(X = r) = nCr pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ; mean np, variance npq.
Poisson: P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ ÷ r!; mean = variance = λ.
Normal: bell-shaped, symmetric about μ; about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 σ.
R functions: dbinom, pbinom, dpois, pnorm, qnorm, rnorm (d density, p cumulative, q quantile, r random).
outcomes: Use R's d, p, q and r functions

topics.title: Correlation and regression
topics.summary: Karl Pearson's correlation and the least-squares regression line.
notes: Regression line of y on x: y − ȳ = b(x − x̄), with b = r × (sᵧ ÷ sₓ).
R: cor(x, y), lm(y ~ x), summary(model).
outcomes: Fit and interpret a regression line in R

topics.title: Hypothesis testing
topics.summary: Null and alternative hypotheses, t-test and chi-square test.
notes: Reject H₀ when the p-value is below the significance level α (often 0.05).
t.test compares means; chisq.test tests independence in a contingency table.
Type I error: rejecting a true H₀; Type II: accepting a false H₀.
outcomes: Run and interpret t and chi-square tests in R

topics.title: Software life cycle models
topics.summary: SDLC phases and the waterfall, prototype, spiral, incremental and agile models.
notes: SDLC phases: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, maintenance.
Waterfall suits stable requirements; prototyping helps when requirements are unclear.
The spiral model is risk-driven; agile delivers working software in short iterations (Scrum sprints).
outcomes: Choose a process model for a project
Explain the phases of the SDLC

topics.title: Requirements and the SRS
topics.summary: Functional and non-functional requirements, elicitation and the SRS document.
notes: Functional requirements say what the system does; non-functional ones say how well (performance, security, usability).
Elicitation: interviews, questionnaires, observation, use cases.
A good SRS is correct, complete, unambiguous, consistent and verifiable.
outcomes: Describe the qualities of a good SRS

topics.title: Design concepts and modelling
topics.summary: Modularity, coupling and cohesion, DFDs and UML diagrams.
notes: Aim for low coupling between modules and high cohesion within them.
DFDs show data flow: processes, data stores, external entities and flows; level 0 is the context diagram.
UML: use case, class, sequence, activity and state diagrams.
outcomes: Draw DFDs and use case diagrams
Judge a design by coupling and cohesion

topics.title: Software testing
topics.summary: Levels and techniques of testing.
notes: Levels: unit, integration, system, acceptance testing.
Black-box testing uses the specification (equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis); white-box testing uses the code (statement, branch, path coverage).
Cyclomatic complexity V(G) = E − N + 2 (edges, nodes) = number of decisions + 1.
outcomes: Design test cases by boundary value analysis

topics.title: Estimation, risk and maintenance
topics.summary: COCOMO, risk management, configuration management and maintenance.
notes: Basic COCOMO: Effort = a(KLOC)^b person-months; organic projects a = 2.4, b = 1.05.
Risk management: identify, analyse, plan and monitor risks.
Maintenance types: corrective, adaptive, perfective, preventive.

topics.title: Cloud computing concepts
topics.summary: Characteristics, service models and deployment models.
notes: NIST characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service.
Service models: IaaS (e.g. virtual machines), PaaS (platforms), SaaS (applications such as e-mail).
Deployment models: public, private, hybrid, community.
outcomes: Classify cloud services by service and deployment model
State the NIST characteristics of cloud computing

topics.title: Virtualisation and containers
topics.summary: Hypervisors, virtual machines and containers.
notes: A type 1 hypervisor runs on bare metal; type 2 runs on a host OS.
Containers share the host kernel and are lighter than VMs.
Virtualisation enables consolidation, isolation and live migration.

topics.title: Cloud platforms, storage and security
topics.summary: Major providers, storage types and the shared responsibility model.
notes: Major platforms: AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud.
Storage: object (e.g. S3), block and file storage.
Shared responsibility: the provider secures the cloud; the customer secures what they put in it.
outcomes: Choose a storage type for an application

courses.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, BCA Semester 6

topics.title: AI, agents and problem solving
topics.summary: Definitions of AI, intelligent agents and state-space search.
notes: An agent perceives its environment through sensors and acts through actuators.
A problem is defined by an initial state, actions, a goal test and path cost.
The Turing test judges whether a machine's conversation is indistinguishable from a human's.
outcomes: Formulate a problem as a state-space search

topics.title: Uninformed and informed search
topics.summary: BFS, DFS, heuristic search and A*.
notes: BFS is complete and optimal for unit costs; DFS uses less memory but may not terminate on infinite paths.
A* expands the node with the lowest f(n) = g(n) + h(n); it is optimal if h never overestimates (admissible).
Hill climbing can get stuck at local maxima.
outcomes: Trace A* on a small graph
Compare BFS, DFS and heuristic search

topics.title: Logic and knowledge representation
topics.summary: Propositional and predicate logic, rules and semantic networks.
notes: Knowledge can be represented by logic, production rules, semantic networks and frames.
Inference: modus ponens (from p and p → q, infer q); resolution.
Forward chaining reasons from facts to goals; backward chaining from goals to facts.
outcomes: Represent knowledge in logic and rules

topics.title: Supervised and unsupervised learning
topics.summary: Regression, classification, clustering and model evaluation.
notes: Supervised learning uses labelled data (regression, classification); unsupervised finds structure in unlabelled data (clustering).
Algorithms: linear regression, decision trees, k-nearest neighbours, naive Bayes, k-means.
Accuracy = (TP + TN) ÷ total; precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP); recall = TP ÷ (TP + FN).
Overfitting: a model fits training data but generalises poorly; use train/test splits and cross-validation.
outcomes: Choose a learning approach for a problem
Evaluate a classifier with a confusion matrix

topics.title: Neural networks
topics.summary: Perceptrons, activation functions and multilayer networks.
notes: A perceptron computes a weighted sum plus bias and applies an activation function.
Activations: step, sigmoid, ReLU, softmax.
Multilayer networks are trained by backpropagation and gradient descent.
outcomes: Explain how a neural network learns

courses.title: Web Programming with PHP and MySQL, BCA Semester 6

topics.title: HTML, CSS and JavaScript essentials
topics.summary: Structure, style and behaviour of web pages.
notes: HTML gives structure (headings, lists, tables, forms); CSS styles it (selectors, box model); JavaScript adds behaviour.
Form method GET sends data in the URL; POST sends it in the request body.
The client–server model: the browser requests, the web server responds over HTTP.

topics.title: PHP syntax, variables and control structures
topics.summary: Embedding PHP, variables, data types, operators, arrays and functions.
notes: PHP runs on the server; code sits inside <?php ... ?>; variables start with $.
Arrays: indexed, associative ($a['name']) and multidimensional; foreach iterates them.
String functions: strlen, str_replace, substr, strtoupper; . concatenates strings.
outcomes: Write PHP scripts with arrays and functions

topics.title: Handling forms and state
topics.summary: $_GET, $_POST, validation, sessions and cookies.
notes: Superglobals $_GET, $_POST and $_REQUEST hold form data.
Validate and sanitise input (htmlspecialchars, filter_var) to prevent XSS.
session_start() begins a session ($_SESSION); setcookie() stores data in the browser.

topics.title: Database access with PHP
topics.summary: Connecting with mysqli or PDO, CRUD operations and prepared statements.
notes: Connect with mysqli_connect or new PDO(dsn, user, password).
Prepared statements with bound parameters prevent SQL injection.
CRUD: INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE from PHP pages.
outcomes: Build a CRUD application with PHP and MySQL
Prevent SQL injection with prepared statements
